title: Om tat sat (17.23–17.28)
hook: three short words that begin and bless an action

segments.voice: Yesterday, food: food, sacrifice, austerity and gift, three kinds each. Today, three words that close the chapter.

Before a runner starts, she touches the line. Before a pianist plays, a breath, hands in the lap. Before a family eats, some pause, some say a word. People mark the start of things that matter. Chapter seventeen has spent a whole day sorting actions into three kinds. At the very end, it offers three words, not for sorting, but for beginning. Om. Tat. Sat. You've met the first one already. It was your second word, back in camp one, the sound before words.
screen: `TOUCH THE LINE.` → `A BREATH BEFORE THE FIRST NOTE.` → `THREE WORDS TO BEGIN.`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-three. Om tat sat: this is remembered as the threefold name of Brahman, the ultimate. By it, long ago, the priests, the Vedas and the sacrifices were set in order. Then Krishna explains each word. Om first. Verse twenty-four: those who follow the Veda always begin their acts of sacrifice, giving and discipline by saying om. The sound goes first. Tat means that. Verse twenty-five: with tat, people seeking freedom do their sacrifice, discipline and giving without aiming at the reward. It's a way of saying, this isn't for me; it's for that. And sat means real, true, good. Verse twenty-six: sat is used for what is real and what is good, and for any praiseworthy act. Verse twenty-seven: steadiness in sacrifice, discipline and giving is called sat, and so is any action done for its sake. So the three words make a small arc. Om: begin with the sacred sound. Tat: offer it to that, not to yourself. Sat: let it be real and good. Then the chapter's last verse, twenty-eight, is a warning that ties back to faith. Whatever is offered, given or practiced without faith is called asat, unreal. It counts for nothing, here or after. The Sanskrit prefix a means not, so asat is simply not-sat. Some printed editions also set these three words in each chapter's closing line, a way of handing the chapter back.
screen: `THE THREEFOLD NAME.` · `OM: BEGIN WITH THE SOUND.` · `TAT: FOR THAT, NOT FOR ME.` · `SAT: REAL AND GOOD.` · then, large: `OM TAT SAT.`

segments.voice: Think of one ordinary thing you'll do after this: cooking, a call, a task at work. Take the first breath as om, the beginning; the second as tat, this isn't only for me; the third as sat, may it be real and good. If you'd like, say the three words softly, then just sit, and let the action wait.
Sat, the real, the good. Gita seventeen, twenty-three: the threefold name of the ultimate, om tat sat; om is the sacred sound, tat is that, and sat is the real and good.
Your line: begin, offer, make it real. Three short words to begin with. Tomorrow, the Gita's last chapter.

howItsDone: Some Hindus say 'om tat sat' at the close of a reading, a ritual or a teaching; some printed Gitas set the three words in each chapter's closing line, and verse 17.24 says Vedic rites begin with om.

myth: om tat sat is called the threefold name of Brahman in Gita 17.23
by it the priests, the Vedas and the sacrifices were set in order.
sat means only 'existence' and has nothing to do with goodness
verse 26: sat is used for what is real and what is good, and for praiseworthy acts.
the Gita says acts done without faith still count fully
verse 28: they're called asat, and count for nothing, here or after.

fork.setup: you're about to begin an act of giving and you want it to be for that, not for you. which word does verse 25 attach to this?
fork.reveal: tat, that. seekers of freedom act with tat, without aiming at the reward.

original.note: Sanskrit: om (the sacred syllable), tat (that), sat (the real, the good); the threefold name in Gita 17.23.

trapdoor: what you thought: om tat sat is a chant with no clear meaning.
what it means: three words that begin an act with the sacred sound, offer it to that, and name it real and good.
what a scholar hears: 17.23 calls it the triple designation (nirdesha) of Brahman; 17.28 names acts without shraddha asat; the phrase recurs in the chapter colophons of some editions.
guess: what is real and true, and also good
a seated posture held during meditation
the last verse that closes a temple chant

notes: 'In many editions... these three words appear at the close of every chapter': chapter colophons in many editions include 'om tat sat'; confirm wording for the edition the path uses.
